  function initializeReadingPreferences() {

    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {

<article class="ltx_document ltx_authors_1line">
<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">RPU – A Reasoning Processing Unit</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Matthew Joseph Adiletta, Gu-Yeon Wei and David Brooks
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>
Harvard University

</span>
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>
</span></span></span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">HPCA 2026 Submission
<span id="id1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">#1268</span>
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>
Confidential Draft 
<br class="ltx_break">Do NOT Distribute!!

</span>
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>
</span></span></span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Large language model (LLM) inference performance is increasingly bottlenecked by the memory wall.
While GPUs continue to scale raw compute throughput, they struggle to deliver scalable performance for memory bandwidth bound workloads.
This challenge is amplified by emerging reasoning LLM applications, where long output sequences, low arithmetic intensity, and tight latency constraints demand significantly higher memory bandwidth.
As a result, system utilization drops and energy per inference rises, highlighting the need for an optimized system architecture for scalable memory bandwidth.</p>
    
<p id="abstract1.2" class="ltx_p">To address these challenges we present the Reasoning Processing Unit (RPU), a chiplet-based architecture designed to address the challenges of the modern memory wall.
RPU introduces:
(1) A Capacity-Optimized High-Bandwidth Memory (HBM-CO) that trades capacity for lower energy and cost;
(2) a scalable chiplet architecture featuring a bandwidth-first power and area provisioning design; and
(3) a decoupled microarchitecture that separates memory, compute, and communication pipelines to sustain high bandwidth utilization.
Simulation results show that RPU performs up to 45.3× lower latency and 18.6× higher throughput over an H100 system at ISO-TDP on Llama3-405B.</p>
  
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">I </span><span id="S1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Introduction</span></h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Low-latency inference is critical for reasoning LLMs, which may generate thousands of tokens before reaching a final answer <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib54" title="" class="ltx_ref">67</a>, <a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>, <a href="#bib.bib56" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a>, <a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">66</a>]</cite>.
Without fast token generation, reasoning tasks become slow, limiting the adoption of this powerful inference approach.
Therefore, we introduce the Reasoning Processing Unit (RPU), a new chiplet-based system architecture that delivers orders of magnitude higher memory bandwidth than today’s compute-centric designs, addressing the core latency bottleneck in reasoning LLMs.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The first step toward low-latency LLM inference is to separate prefill and decode onto different systems, as in Dynamo <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib62" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>]</cite> and the Splitwise execution model <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib68" title="" class="ltx_ref">50</a>]</cite>.
Prefill is compute-bound and highly parallel, making it efficient to run on today’s GPU architectures.
Decode, in contrast, is inherently sequential and latency-sensitive.
When prioritizing latency, decode systems must operate at low batch sizes, often as low as one.
This low-batch regime is not a choice but a necessity, for two key reasons.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">First, each query must compute attention sequentially during decode, so larger batch sizes lead to higher latencies.
Long sequences are common in reasoning models, which makes this effect even more pronounced.
Second, latency-optimized techniques like speculative decoding <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib59" title="" class="ltx_ref">34</a>]</cite> are only effective at low batch sizes <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">14</a>]</cite>.
As a result, small batch sizes are essential for low latency.
However, low-batch inference exacerbates the memory wall problem.
For example, Figure 1 shows low-batch decode operates far below the H100’s compute roofline.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S1.F1" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18568v1/rpu-vs-h100-roofline.svg" id="S1.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/238;" width="476" height="238"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Fig. 1: </span>RPU provides higher memory bandwidth than H100, which is required for low-latency decoding. Even up to BS=32, arithmetic intensity remains low, but requires the RPU to execute kernels which straddle the roofline.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">System architects have responded to the decode bottleneck by cramming more HBM stacks into each package as the simplest way to chase bandwidth <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>, <a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">61</a>, <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">63</a>, <a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">24</a>]</cite>.
However, HBM was not designed for inference.
Its popularity was driven primarily by GPU training, pushing a roadmap focused on high bandwidth coupled with high capacity to store massive training datasets and large model checkpoints to feed dense compute architectures.
Now, as applications shift toward inference, HBM’s high capacity per module drives up energy and cost, undermining scalability for low-latency inference.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Challenge 1 – Energy and Cost of Memory.</span>
In streaming workloads, over 74% of memory device energy is spent moving data across long internal wires and TSVs within the DRAM stack <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib60" title="" class="ltx_ref">45</a>, <a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">40</a>]</cite>.
Higher capacity HBMs increase internal paths, driving up energy per bit.
This creates a fundamental mismatch for low-reuse
streaming workloads, where minimizing energy per bit is critical for efficiency.
Similarly, the cost of next-generation AI accelerators is increasingly dominated by HBM memory <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">49</a>, <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">48</a>]</cite>.
Cost scales with capacity, as larger stacks require more silicon area and complex packaging.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">The capacity required per socket depends on how a model is deployed (e.g., a single node, across a rack <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">43</a>]</cite>, or at datacenter scale <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">23</a>]</cite>).
If a model fits in one GPU, doubling the number of sockets doubles bandwidth, but it also halves the capacity needed per socket.
We call this the <span id="S1.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">memory overprovisioning paradox</span>: a system-level design inefficiency where scaling out for bandwidth to achieve lower latency overprovisions capacity and drives up system cost and energy.
The correct architectural approach is to provision memory based on the scale of the intended deployment.
But with HBM as the only high-bandwidth memory available <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">26</a>]</cite>, architects are locked into a costly compromise – <span id="S1.p6.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">buying bandwidth with capacity</span>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p7.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.p7.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">Contribution 1 – HBM-CO: An HBM-style memory design which can be optimized to the bandwidth-capacity needs of low-batch LLMs, addressing energy and cost challenges of the memory wall (Section <a href="#S3" title="III Capacity Optimized High Bandwidth Memory ‣ RPU – A Reasoning Processing Unit" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">III</span></a>).</span>
HBM-CO retains HBM’s internal bandwidth architecture and shoreline bandwidth, but selectively reduces capacity-driving structures such as ranks, banks and subarrays to optimize for the capacity needs of low-latency inference.
These changes require minimal modification to the HBM stack, making HBM-CO a practical and manufacturable design point.
This yields higher bandwidth per dollar and up to 2.4× energy efficiency than conventional HBM, despite a higher cost per GB.
We quantify these tradeoffs using an analytical modeling approach based on <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib60" title="" class="ltx_ref">45</a>]</cite>, which estimates energy per bit and cost per module from wire-length scaling trends from HBM core-die floorplans <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">32</a>, <a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">54</a>, <a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">47</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p8.1" class="ltx_p">Modularizing memory with HBM-CO unlocks a new design regime.
Instead of provisioning large, monolithic capacity per socket, systems can scale bandwidth and capacity across many smaller stacks.
But this flexibility introduces a new architectural challenge: how do we build a compute fabric that can glue together these HBM-CO modules, deliver the desired bandwidth, and stay within tight power and packaging limits?
The answer requires rethinking how power and area are provisioned in modern accelerators.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p9" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p9.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.p9.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Challenge 2 – Power and Area Provisioning for A Scalable Compute Fabric:</span>
Today’s HBM-based accelerators (e.g., H100 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>]</cite>, MI300x <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">61</a>]</cite>) allocate only 30-40% of system thermal design power (TDP) to memory interfaces, meaning that memory-bound workloads leave a large fraction of available power underutilized.
These systems are also reticle-limited, which favor dense compute, but this leads to overprovisioned arithmetic and cache resources during bandwidth bound workloads.
Additionally, memory bandwidth scales with die perimeter, not area, because each HBM stack requires a dense ring of high-speed IOs along the chip edge (shoreline) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>]</cite>.
Reticle-limited designs minimize this perimeter-to-area ratio, which directly conflicts with the need for scalable bandwidth.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p10" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p10.1" class="ltx_p">Alternatively, accelerators like Cerebras <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">64</a>]</cite> and Groq <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>]</cite> avoid shoreline constraints by using SRAM as main memory.
However, SRAM’s low density drives up power, cost, and infrastructure overheads.
For example, Cerebras requires four WSEs to host a 70B model, and Groq needs hundreds of processors.
In contrast, DRAM provides the density to support large models at far lower system footprint.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p11" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p11.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.p11.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">Contribution 2 – RPU: A modular chiplet-based architecture that dedicates more power to memory interfaces and optimizes the compute-to-bandwidth ratio for low-latency token generation (Section <a href="#S4" title="IV Compute Fabric for Low-Latency Inference ‣ RPU – A Reasoning Processing Unit" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">IV</span></a>).</span>
The RPU embraces emerging trends in package-level integration to achieve scalable memory bandwidth.
Rather than concentrating compute in a monolithic die, the RPU distributes compute across many smaller chiplets.
As a result, for the same compute die area, the RPU exposes nearly 10× more memory IO shoreline than the H100 (600mm vs. 60mm), enabling tighter coupling between memory and logic.
Four compute chiplets are co-packaged with eight HBM-CO stacks, following package-level integration strategies pioneered by modern GPU architectures <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>, <a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">61</a>, <a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">52</a>, <a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">23</a>, <a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">16</a>]</cite>.
Packages are composed at the board level, increasing bandwidth until blade-level power envelopes.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p12" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p12.1" class="ltx_p">In parallel, the RPU reprovisions power and area.
The RPU dedicates 70-80% of power to memory interfaces.
This keeps the memory bandwidth bound power near the peak power and enables over 2× bandwidth at ISO TDP versus compute-centric GPUs.
The RPU also aligns the compute-to-bandwidth ratio.
By removing underutilized compute and cache resources, it improves area efficiency and reduces die cost.
As shown in Figure <a href="#S1.F1" title="Fig. 1 ‣ I Introduction ‣ RPU – A Reasoning Processing Unit" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, these RPU design choices shift the roofline down and to the left, which is a better fit for low-latency inference.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p13" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p13.1" class="ltx_p">The RPU system-architecture make more bandwidth available; however, roofline availability is not the same as utilization.
Realizing the full potential of the RPU system requires rethinking how we sustain bandwidth at scale.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p14" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p14.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.p14.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Challenge 3 – Utilizing the Newly Available Bandwidth:</span>
Today’s systems struggle to use memory bandwidth effectively, particularly in low-batch LLM token generation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib63" title="" class="ltx_ref">68</a>, <a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">30</a>]</cite>.
This is because small, distributed weight matrices limit streaming bandwidth <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">35</a>, <a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">52</a>]</cite>.
For example, the fused <span id="S1.p14.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">gate/up</span> projection MLP layer in Llama4-Maverick contains just 168 million parameters <span id="S1.p14.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">(5k×32k)</span>.
When <span id="S1.p14.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">column-sharded</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib70" title="" class="ltx_ref">65</a>]</cite> across devices with TB/s of bandwidth, the roofline model predicts runtimes in the tens of microseconds.
In practice, kernel launch and tensor-parallel communication latencies are often of similar magnitude, which limit bandwidth utilization <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">35</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p15" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p15.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.p15.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">Contribution 3 – Reasoning Core: A decoupled pipeline microarchitecture and custom ISA that fully saturates available memory bandwidth (Section <a href="#S5" title="V Micro-Architecture ‣ RPU – A Reasoning Processing Unit" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">V</span></a>).</span>
Achieving high bandwidth utilization requires careful orchestration of data movement.
The RPU Reasoning Core microarchitecture addresses this by separating dataflow for memory, compute, and network into independent pipelines, connected by on-chip buffers and coordinated through programmable pipeline arbiters.
This decoupling allows each pipeline to make forward progress based on data readiness, without stalling on global barriers.
At batch size 1 <span id="S1.p15.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">(BS=1)</span>, the RPU saturates memory bandwidth and achieves roofline performance.
On the other hand, batch size 32 <span id="S1.p15.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">(BS=32)</span>, contains kernels that straddle the roofline, as shown in Figure 1, alternating between memory-bound SDPA and MoE layers and compute-bound Linear layers.
Decoupled pipelines enable the RPU to absorb this phase imbalance into the buffer hierarchy and sustain throughput at the workloads average arithmetic intensity (AI).</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p16" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p16.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.p16.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">Contribution 4: An end-to-end simulation framework for LLM inference on RPU (Sections <a href="#S6" title="VI RPU Software Stack and Simulation ‣ RPU – A Reasoning Processing Unit" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">VI</span></a>- <a href="#S8" title="VIII Strong Scaling Analysis ‣ RPU – A Reasoning Processing Unit" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">VIII</span></a>).</span>
We developed a simulation framework, combining RTL-modeled compute kernels, an analytical energy model of HBM-CO memory, and an event-driven simulator <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">55</a>, <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>]</cite> that executes compiled LLM workloads via a custom RPU ISA.
This framework captures transient dataflows, pipeline utilization, and synchronization stalls, which enables detailed architectural comparisons against modern GPUs.
Compared to an H100 at ISO-TDP, RPU achieves up to 45.3× lower latency and 18.6× higher throughput on Llama3-405B at similar system cost.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S1.F2" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18568v1/replot_llama_70b_75s_to_250s.svg" id="S1.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:329/125;" width="329" height="125"></object></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18568v1/vmm_bw_util_scatter_only_h100.svg" id="S1.F2.g2" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:143/125;" width="143" height="125"></object></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Fig. 2: </span>Power and utilization characterization of H100 using NVML.
Left: Power trace during distributed inference (4xH100) of Llama3-70B (Batch=32).
Right: Isolated kernel profiling for memory bandwidth utilization across batch sizes and matrix dimensions (BF16). </figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="S1.F3" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18568v1/dgemm_power_h100.svg" id="S1.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/208;" width="476" height="208"></object>

</figure>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">II </span><span id="S2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Motivation for a Decode-Optimized System</span></h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To illustrate the challenges of the modern memory wall on today’s GPUs, we profile the H100 using: (1) low batch LLM inference for end-to-end behavior, and (2) standalone dense-linear kernels to isolate bottlenecks.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">Experimental Setup:</span>
We use NVIDIA’s NVML <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">44</a>]</cite> to measure power on an H100 GPU running CUDA software stacks optimized for HBM3e.
For full-model profiling, we profile Llama-70B with FP8 weights <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">41</a>]</cite> on 4×H100s using vLLM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib58" title="" class="ltx_ref">31</a>]</cite> and NVIDIA Dynamo <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib62" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>]</cite>, running batch-32 inference with 16k prefill and 2k decode tokens (Figure <a href="#S1.F2" title="Fig. 2 ‣ I Introduction ‣ RPU – A Reasoning Processing Unit" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, left).
To isolate bottlenecks, we also benchmark representative dense-linear kernels compiled with PyTorch 2.2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">22</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">Low Power Efficiency at Low Batch Sizes:</span>
Figure <a href="#S1.F2" title="Fig. 2 ‣ I Introduction ‣ RPU – A Reasoning Processing Unit" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> (left) shows that during LLM prefill, the H100 uses 90% of its TDP and achieves high compute utilization.
In contrast, the decode-phase only uses 34% of its TDP.
This observation is reinforced by isolated dense-linear profiling in Figure <a href="#S1.F3" title="Fig. 3 ‣ I Introduction ‣ RPU – A Reasoning Processing Unit" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> (left); batch sizes <math id="S2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\leq" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>≤</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\leq</annotation></semantics></math>64 consistently yield <math id="S2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="&lt;" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>&lt;</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">&lt;</annotation></semantics></math>30% TDP.
The inability to fully utilize power suggests a critical mismatch between the H100 design and low-latency inference.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">Low Energy Efficiency at Low Batch Sizes:</span>
Figure <a href="#S1.F3" title="Fig. 3 ‣ I Introduction ‣ RPU – A Reasoning Processing Unit" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> (right) shows that while high AI, compute-bound kernels are energy efficient (<math id="S2.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>1.0 pJ/BF16 FLOP), this degrades by 10-1000× for low-batch inference due to non-amortized data movement costs.
HBM3e accesses alone account for 30-50% of total energy <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">40</a>]</cite>, with additional losses from on-chip data movement across the H100’s large monolithic die <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>]</cite>.
The UMA memory system and randomized address mapping further inflate energy costs by
physically increasing the distance data travels from memory to compute.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">Inference Does Not Achieve Peak Memory-BW Utilization: </span>
Our profiling shows
that the H100 only utilizes 32% of its peak memory bandwidth during distributed LLM decode.
This observation is consistent with prior work on low-batch inference <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">52</a>, <a href="#bib.bib63" title="" class="ltx_ref">68</a>, <a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">30</a>]</cite> as well as NVIDIA self-reported benchmarks (20k/2k at 911 OTPS) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">44</a>]</cite>.
Isolated experiments in Figure <a href="#S1.F2" title="Fig. 2 ‣ I Introduction ‣ RPU – A Reasoning Processing Unit" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> (right) show that full bandwidth is only achieved when the working set exceeds <math id="S2.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>1GB, which is far larger than typical LLM matrices.
Model sharding and reduced precision (e.g., 16-bit to 4-bit) further reduces each matrix’s footprint per GPU, leading to even lower bandwidth utilization.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Multiple factors contribute to low memory bandwidth utilization: kernel launch overheads become non-negligible for small kernel sizes <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">35</a>]</cite>; long memory access latencies cannot be hidden behind compute; and inefficient vector broadcasts between SMs using shared memory limit throughput between layers.
Together, these limitations show that the H100 memory system is not optimized for the decode phase of LLMs, underscoring the need for a decode optimized architecture.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">III </span><span id="S3.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Capacity Optimized High Bandwidth Memory</span></h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Low-batch token generation latency is fundamentally limited by memory bandwidth.
For dense models like Llama3, consider the case where the model’s memory footprint (weights and KV$) fits perfectly within the systems memory capacity (100% capacity utilization).
In this configuration, all memory capacity is actively used, and token generation latency is determined solely by how quickly that memory can be read.
This scenario exposes a fundamental constraint: when memory is fully utilized, the minimum achievable latency is set by the ratio of bandwidth to capacity (BW/Cap).
As a result, BW/Cap emerges as a key metric for evaluating and designing memory systems for bandwidth-bound inference.
Higher BW/Cap enables faster access to the entire model, reducing latency and improving memory efficiency.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Modern memory systems fall short of the bandwidth-to-capacity ratios desirable for efficient low-latency inference.
For example, achieving a 1ms token latency while fully utilizing memory would require a BW/Cap of approximately 1000, which is equivalent to 1TB/s per GB.
In contrast, high-end memory technologies like HBM3e offer much lower BW/Cap ratios. For instance, a single HBM3e stack provides 1280GB/s of bandwidth and 48GB of capacity, yielding a BW/Cap of 27 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">32</a>]</cite>.
To meet bandwidth targets, system designers must aggregate multiple stacks, which increases total memory capacity far beyond what the model requires and results in severe capacity underutilization.
The fraction of memory actually used is proportional to the ratio between available and required BW/Cap.
In this example, with a target of 1000 and available BW/Cap of 27, only 2.7% of capacity is effectively utilized.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">This mismatch between the desired bandwidth and practical memory capacity defines the memory overprovisioning paradox: High-capacity DRAM-based memories like HBM, GDDR, and LP-DDR <span id="S3.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">buy bandwidth via capacity</span> – scaling and distributing weights across multiple memory modules to increase memory bandwidth, resulting in under-utilized capacity.
Conversely, SRAM-based architectures <span id="S3.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">buy capacity via bandwidth</span> – offering extreme bandwidth, but struggling to fully utilize it due to excessive sharding across devices caused by limited storage density.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F4" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18568v1/BW_PER_CAP.png" id="S3.F4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/235;" width="476" height="235" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Fig. 4: </span>
Memory technology landscape comparing bandwidth per capacity versus latency per token with 100% capacity utilization for dense LLMs. A technology gap exists in the <span id="S3.F4.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Goldilocks</span> range for low-latency inference.
</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S3.F4" title="Fig. 4 ‣ III Capacity Optimized High Bandwidth Memory ‣ RPU – A Reasoning Processing Unit" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> illustrates this design gap: no commercial memory technology occupies the high BW/Cap regime desirable for low-latency LLM inference.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Overprovisioned capacity also introduces energy and cost inefficiencies.
Prior work <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib60" title="" class="ltx_ref">45</a>]</cite> shows that 74% of HBM energy in streaming workloads is spent on internal data movement, with only 14% and 12% attributed to I/O and row activation.
As capacity increases, internal wire lengths grow, raising energy per bit and reducing efficiency.
In addition, memory cost scales with capacity due to more silicon area.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p6.1" class="ltx_p">To address these challenges, memory capacity per device should become a tunable architectural parameter.
LLMs differ widely in model size, sparsity, deployment context, and system constraints.
Each use case has a different optimal BW/Cap profile, often beyond what current technologies can deliver.
Decoupling capacity from bandwidth would allow system designers to provision memory precisely for application needs, improving performance, efficiency, and cost-effectiveness.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F5" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18568v1/hbm-co-dse.svg" id="S3.F5.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:467/519;" width="467" height="519"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Fig. 5: </span>Tradeoffs in HBM-CO memories, illustrating that high-BW/Cap memories are up to <math id="S3.F5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>2.5x more energy efficient than an HBM3e device, but <math id="S3.F5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>1.8x the higher cost per GB.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S3.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p7.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p7.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">The Design Space of HBM-CO Memories: </span>
To fill the memory technology gap for low-latency inference, we propose a new class of memory devices: <span id="S3.p7.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Capacity-Optimized High-Bandwidth Memories</span> (HBM-CO).
We analyzed the HBM architecture and identified parameters that impact a stacked memory’s bandwidth-to-capacity ratio <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">5</a>, <a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">27</a>, <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">26</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p8.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p8.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">HBM Ranks and Layers:</span>
Each rank consists of four stacked DRAM layers (dies).
All layers in a rank contribute to higher memory bandwidth, each with separate channels.
However, increasing the number of ranks adds memory capacity but does not increase bandwidth, since the interface is shared.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p9" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p9.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p9.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">HBM Channels and Pseudo-Channels:</span>
A DRAM layer is partitioned into four channels, each of which is further split into two pseudo-channels (pCHs) for a total of eight pCHs per layer.
The 8 pCH across 4 layers per rank fully saturate the memory bandwidth broken into a 32-pCh x 32b IO interface.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p10" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p10.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p10.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">HBM Bank Groups, Banks, and Sub-Arrays:</span>

A pseudo-channel contains four bank groups, each with four banks.
To sustain the full 32 GB/s bandwidth per pCH, only one active bank per bank group is needed
using innovations such as sub-array level parallelism <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">28</a>]</cite>.
Four active bank groups per pCH are pipelined to delivers 256 bits per 1 GHz.
Banks are composed of subarrays, which contribute to total capacity but do not impact bandwidth.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p11" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p11.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p11.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Key Insight to Change the BW/Cap of HBM:</span>
HBMs achieve peak bandwidth per shoreline with just one active bank per bank group per pseudo-channel.
This means capacity structures such as sub-arrays per bank, banks per bank group, and ranks can be parameterized without changing bandwidth.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p12" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p12.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p12.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">Modeling Energy and Cost for HBM-CO: </span>
We developed an analytical HBM-CO model to capture tradeoffs in bandwidth, capacity, energy, and cost.
Energy per bit was broken into four components:
(1) Row Activation: 0.18pJ/bit for streaming workloads <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib60" title="" class="ltx_ref">45</a>, <a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">5</a>]</cite>.
We conservatively model HBM-CO with HBM3 timing and activation energy, leaving potential bandwidth and energy gains from its smaller core-die and sub-arrays for a future physical design study.
(2) Data Movement: 0.2pJ/bit/mm, estimated from intra-die routing distances derived from HBM core-die floorplans <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">32</a>, <a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">54</a>, <a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">47</a>]</cite>.
(3) TSV Traversal: 0.148pJ/bit/layer, based on 0.8pF TSV capacitance and switching energy <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">25</a>]</cite>.
(4) I/O Interface: 0.25pJ/bit, drawn from UCIe specs and HBM3e datasheets <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>, <a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">40</a>]</cite>.
Cost is normalized against an HBM3e baseline <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">49</a>, <a href="#bib.bib63" title="" class="ltx_ref">68</a>]</cite>, scaling against silicon area and accounting for non-amortized costs such as base-die logic and TSV footprint.
At lower capacities, these fixed costs dominate, impacting cost per GB more significantly.
We validate our HBM-CO model against HBM3e <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">40</a>]</cite> reported 3.44pJ/bit.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F6" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18568v1/PISTIL_DESIGN_FIG_V3.png" id="S3.F6.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:476/590;" width="476" height="590" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Fig. 6: </span>Proposed RPU system architecture for low-latency LLM inference, featuring a chiplet-based design that rebalances compute, memory, and network resources. Each level of the hierarchy, from core micro-architecture to compute units, packages, and ring-station scale-up, is co-optimized for energy-efficient, cost-effective, and scalable memory bandwidth.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S3.p13" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p13.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p13.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">Design Space Takeaways: </span>
Figure <a href="#S3.F5" title="Fig. 5 ‣ III Capacity Optimized High Bandwidth Memory ‣ RPU – A Reasoning Processing Unit" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> visualizes the tradeoffs in energy, cost, and BW/Cap for HBM-CO memories.
A candidate Pareto-optimal HBM-CO memory has 768MB capacity, 256GB/s bandwidth (BW/Cap = 341), and 1.45pJ/bit energy.
This device offers 2.4× lower energy per bit than HBM3e while maintaining the same bandwidth per shoreline (GB/s/mm).
This candidate memory BW/Cap leads to an ideal token latency of <math id="S3.p13.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2.9" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>2.9</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2.9</annotation></semantics></math>ms per token, falling in the middle of the <span id="S3.p13.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Goldilocks</span> memory range of Figure <a href="#S3.F4" title="Fig. 4 ‣ III Capacity Optimized High Bandwidth Memory ‣ RPU – A Reasoning Processing Unit" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>.
An HBM3e system with the same performance would only utilize 7.9% of its capacity for inference with a dense LLM.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F7" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18568v1/VMM_PROCEDURE.png" id="S3.F7.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/324;" width="476" height="324" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Fig. 7: </span>Vector-Tile weight streaming dataflow and VMM procedure following a stripe-based execution.
Arrows in <span id="S3.F7.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Weight Streaming Dataflow</span> indicate how activations and weights are moved into TMAC unit – activations are broadcast across columns while weights are element-wise moved.
The arrows in the <span id="S3.F7.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">VMM Procedure</span> indicates the order tiles are processed – column-wise first until eight rows of tiles are processed, then the next column starts, proceeding until all the columns in a stripe are completed. </figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S3.p14" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p14.1" class="ltx_p">This efficiency comes at a cost.
The candidate is 1.81× more expensive per GB, seemingly violating the foundational DRAM principle of minimizing cost per bit.
However, for low-latency inference, bandwidth per dollar is the important design metric.
By trading 192× capacity and 1.81× higher price per GB, the resulting module is 35× lower cost overall, achieving 5× higher bandwidth per dollar than HBM3e.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">IV </span><span id="S4.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Compute Fabric for Low-Latency Inference</span></h2>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Distributed Vector-Matrix Multiplication (VMM)
is the core operation in LLM token generation.
Given an input vector <math id="S4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V\in\mathbb{R}^{1\times K}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>V</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V\in\mathbb{R}^{1\times K}</annotation></semantics></math> and a weight matrix <math id="S4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W\in\mathbb{R}^{K\times N}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>W</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W\in\mathbb{R}^{K\times N}</annotation></semantics></math>: <math id="S4.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O=V*W,\quad O\in\mathbb{R}^{1\times N}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>V</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">∗</mo><mi>W</mi></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O=V*W,\quad O\in\mathbb{R}^{1\times N}</annotation></semantics></math>.
For low-latency inference, this computation must be parallelized efficiently across devices to maintain fast, per-token response times.
Prior work <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib70" title="" class="ltx_ref">65</a>]</cite> has exploited the layered structure of AI models, where each layer’s output serves as part of the input to the next.
Consider a system comprising <math id="S4.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>C</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C</annotation></semantics></math> number of cores.
Sharding <math id="S4.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>W</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W</annotation></semantics></math> along its columns ensures that each core computes a disjoint portion of the output vector.
The weight matrix is partitioned such that each core stores <math id="S4.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{K\times\frac{N}{C}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mfrac><mi>N</mi><mi>C</mi></mfrac></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{K\times\frac{N}{C}}</annotation></semantics></math> and computes its corresponding output fragment <math id="S4.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O_{i}=V*W_{i},\quad O_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{1\times\frac{N}{C}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>O</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>V</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">∗</mo><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>O</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mfrac><mi>N</mi><mi>C</mi></mfrac></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O_{i}=V*W_{i},\quad O_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{1\times\frac{N}{C}}</annotation></semantics></math></p>
</div>
<div id="S4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Since each core holds a portion of the output vector <math id="S4.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>O</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O</annotation></semantics></math>, which serves as the input to the next layer (<math id="S4.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>O</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> becomes <math id="S4.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V_{i}</annotation></semantics></math>), it can immediately begin computing on its local fragment for the next layer while simultaneously broadcasting its portion of <math id="S4.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>V</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V</annotation></semantics></math> to other cores.
This allows each core to progress with available data while receiving the remaining parts of <math id="S4.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>V</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V</annotation></semantics></math>.
This strategy mirrors Cannon’s algorithm for distributed matrix multiplication, where data movement and computation are interleaved to maximize efficiency.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p3.1" class="ltx_p">To further increase parallelism, rows of <math id="S4.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>W</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W</annotation></semantics></math> (<math id="S4.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math>-dimension) can be distributed across <math id="S4.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>G</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">G</annotation></semantics></math> cores in a processing groups.
Using this approach, each core stores weight shard <math id="S4.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{j,i}\in\mathbb{R}^{\frac{K}{G}\times\frac{N}{C/G}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mfrac><mi>K</mi><mi>G</mi></mfrac><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mfrac><mi>N</mi><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>/</mo><mi>G</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{j,i}\in\mathbb{R}^{\frac{K}{G}\times\frac{N}{C/G}}</annotation></semantics></math> to compute a partial output <math id="S4.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O_{j,i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O_{j,i}</annotation></semantics></math>, requiring a reduction step to sum the intermediate results <math id="S4.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O_{i}=\sum_{j=1}^{G}O_{j,i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>O</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mrow><msubsup><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>G</mi></msubsup><msub><mi>O</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O_{i}=\sum_{j=1}^{G}O_{j,i}</annotation></semantics></math>.
This reduction will always appear on the compute-network critical path, unlike the prior network-broadcast.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S3.F6" title="Fig. 6 ‣ III Capacity Optimized High Bandwidth Memory ‣ RPU – A Reasoning Processing Unit" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> illustrates the proposed RPU chiplet-based architecture, designed to accelerate distributed VMM for low-latency inference.
The RPU tightly integrates compute and memory across multiple hierarchy levels – cores, compute units, packages, and ring stations – to form a scalable and efficient system architecture.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">Compute Unit and Reasoning Core: </span>
The Compute Unit (CU) is the fundamental building block of the RPU, providing tightly coupled compute and memory resources.
Each CU is constructed with one compute chiplet and two HBM-CO chiplets, connected through advanced packaging such as EMIB <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib67" title="" class="ltx_ref">37</a>]</cite> or CoWoS-L <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">21</a>]</cite>.
The module provides dual 256 GB/s memory shorelines, delivering consistent bandwidth per interface while offering customizable HBM-CO capacity.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p6.1" class="ltx_p">The particular HBM-CO chiplet visualized in Figure <a href="#S3.F6" title="Fig. 6 ‣ III Capacity Optimized High Bandwidth Memory ‣ RPU – A Reasoning Processing Unit" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> is derived from the HBM core-die shown in Figure 2 of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">47</a>]</cite>, compacted by reducing banks per group from four to one, ranks from four to one, channels per layer from four to one, but keeping four layers per rank.
Physically, the design reduces the DRAM array region and channel shoreline proportionally, while the TSV, command, and peripheral logic regions are unscaled, occupying roughly one-third of the total die area.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p7.1" class="ltx_p">The compute-to-bandwidth ratio for a CU was determined empirically for low-latency inference using MXFP4 formats.
We found that 32 OPs/Byte maximized utilization (Figure <a href="#S1.F1" title="Fig. 1 ‣ I Introduction ‣ RPU – A Reasoning Processing Unit" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>); higher ratios offered little benefit and only increased design complexity, silicon area, and energy cost.
Thus, each 256 GB/s shoreline requires 8 TOPs of compute throughput.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p8.1" class="ltx_p">The 256 GB/s shoreline can easily accommodate 512 MAC units along the same horizontal span while leaving adequate space for routing – defining the <span id="S4.p8.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">compute shoreline</span>.
To reach the target 8 TOPs, we stack 16 rows of MACs, organized into 8 reasoning cores.
Each reasoning core comprises four 8x8 tile-multipliers (TMACs) and connects to its own HBM-CO memory pseudo-channel delivering 32 GB/s of memory bandwidth.
This vertical stacking keeps routing paths short and avoids congestion along the bandwidth edge.
Using both the top and bottom chip edges doubles the number of cores per CU while preserving a balanced area-to-perimeter ratio.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.p9" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p9.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.p9.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">Package Architecture: </span>
Four CUs are integrated onto a single package substrate, each equipped with its pair of dedicated HBM-CO memories offering 2 TB/s of memory bandwidth.
At the package level, compute chiplets form a segment of the <span id="S4.p9.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">outer ring</span> hierarchy.
Vector fragments within a CU are forwarded to neighboring CUs in the same package through energy-efficient, short-reach UCIe interconnects <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>]</cite>.
To minimize communication latency, each core includes a custom DMA engine optimized for fast inter-chiplet transfers, achieving latencies of <math id="S4.p9.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\leq" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>≤</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\leq</annotation></semantics></math>10 ns per CU-to-CU hop, which is similar to prior works <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">58</a>, <a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">71</a>, <a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>, <a href="#bib.bib61" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>]</cite>.
Each compute chiplet uses a unified UCIe-S physical interface with segmented drivers: in-package links run at low voltage and high frequency (0.5 pJ/bit), while off-package links operate up to 16 GT/s with 0.75-1.2 pJ/bit energy<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>, <a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">51</a>]</cite>, defining the system’s outer-ring bandwidth at 128 GB/s/mm.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.p10" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p10.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.p10.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">RPU Scale-Up: </span>
Multiple packages are soldered onto a PCB to form the outer ring topology, connected via a Ring Station.
Communication between packages leverages PCB-routed interconnects, designed specifically for short-reach (<math id="S4.p10.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="&lt;" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>&lt;</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">&lt;</annotation></semantics></math>10 mm) data transfers.
A secondary purpose of the Ring-Station is to network outside the system (e.g., 100Gb Ethernet).</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.p11" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p11.1" class="ltx_p">An RPU is defined as a scalable compute system, composed of multiple co-packaged CUs, assembled on a board.
Similar to how GPUs scale across datacenter and edge deployments by varying the number of CUDA cores, RPUs scale by composing different numbers of CUs.
Our modular architecture enables flexible configurations to meet diverse performance, capacity, energy, and cost targets.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">V </span><span id="S5.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Micro-Architecture</span></h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">NUMA Domains and Data Dependent Synchronization: </span>
A central design principle of our microarchitecture is a fully NUMA-based system.
Each compute core within a CU forms an independent NUMA domain, without shared memory between cores.
All data movement across domains is explicitly managed via software-programmable DMA engines and data-dependenct synchronization.
This eliminates coherence overhead, enables deterministic execution, and ensures scalable performance for dataflow-dominated workloads like LLM inference.
Thus, the RPU favors <span id="S5.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">bespoke datapaths over generalized programming models.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">NUMA at All Scales: </span>
Each core includes three programmable data pipelines, each operating within its local NUMA boundary.
The Memory DMA transfers data between the core’s dedicated HBM-CO memory channel and its memory buffer. The Compute DMA reads from memory or network buffers and feeds data into the compute pipeline.
The Network DMAs manage all inter-core and inter-chiplet communication, linking each core to neighboring cores within a CU and the positionally aligned core in adjacent CUs. Incoming data is written to the network buffer and may be consumed locally and/or forwarded using custom forwarding instructions. This supports efficient collectives and data reuse across chiplets.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">Pipeline Arbiters: </span>
We developed Pipeline Arbiters to synchronize decoupled memory, compute, and network pipelines.
These lightweight, software-managed mechanisms are embedded within each core’s SRAM buffer.
Each SRAM buffer entry includes a 2-bit valid counter that tracks the expected number of asynchronous consumers.
DMA operations are programmed with a <span id="S5.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">valid_count</span> when writing and may optionally enable a <span id="S5.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">check_valid</span> flag to stall if the target address is occupied.
On the read side, consumers can use <span id="S5.p3.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">check_valid</span> to stall until data is ready and optionally decrement the valid counter after access.
For example, a Network DMA may set <span id="S5.p3.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">valid_count=2</span> since activations will be consumed by (1) the compute pipeline and (2) asynchronously forwarded to neighboring cores.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p4.1" class="ltx_p">To guarantee mutual exclusion, each buffer entry is accessed through a hardware-enforced arbitration mechanism that serializes requests from multiple consumers.
Accesses are prioritized using a software-configurable policy, ensuring that only one DMA engine can read, write, or update the valid counter at a time.
This enforces atomicity at the buffer-entry level and prevents race conditions across the memory, compute, and network pipelines.
By managing synchronization through software-defined counters and flags, Pipeline Arbiters enable fine-grained, data-driven execution between NUMA domains with blocking and non-blocking semantics.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">TMAC and HP-VOPs: </span>
The vector-tile MAC (TMAC) is the core computational unit for accelerating the VMM kernel, as shown in Figure <a href="#S3.F7" title="Fig. 7 ‣ III Capacity Optimized High Bandwidth Memory ‣ RPU – A Reasoning Processing Unit" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>.
Each TMAC consists of 64 MAC units arranged in an 8×8 array, performing BF16 multiplies with FP32 accumulations.
This structure allows one activation vector to be broadcast across 8 columns of the weight matrix, computing 64 MACs per cycle using a weight-streaming, output-stationary dataflow.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p6.1" class="ltx_p">To maximize on-chip reuse of activation data and minimize accumulation write-back pressure, the VMM algorithm is organized into stripes.
A stripe is a groups of 8 vertically stacked tiles spanning all columns of the weight shard.
Activation shards per stripe contains 64 BF16 values, stored in a dedicated register file close to the tile multipliers.
These values are initially fetched from the network buffer, then reused across all tile columns before being retired.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p7.1" class="ltx_p">The tile multipliers first iterate over the tile-rows within a stripe.
After processing a column of tiles, the accumulated face is reduced via a column-wise (3-stage) tree sum.
These results are written back to a local register file to be read back for the next stripe, leveraging the fact that each core typically operates on small output shards (<math id="S5.p7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="&lt;" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>&lt;</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">&lt;</annotation></semantics></math>256 elements) in highly distributed VMMs.
Once all the weight matrix columns of a stripe are computed, the next activation stripe shard is loaded from the network buffer, and the process repeats.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p8.1" class="ltx_p">This striping approach is essential for three reasons:
(1) Traversing columns first (inner-product style) would require the full activation vector to be stored on-chip, stalling compute during the vector broadcast across all CUs.
(2) Traversing rows first (outer-product style) would result in high writeback bandwidth due to frequent partial sum updates.
(3) By processing one stripe at a time, we minimize on-chip bandwidth requirements and enable fine-grained overlap of computation and communication; the next activation shard is collected in the network buffer while compute works on the current shard.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p9" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p9.1" class="ltx_p">In addition to the tile multipliers, each core includes a general-purpose, high-precision (FP32) vector operations (HP-VOPs) accelerator, enabling support for key functions in LLM workloads (e.g., SiLU, GeLU, normalization, and rotary embeddings).
Because overall performance is dominated by memory bandwidth, we can afford to allocate area to high-precision computation without significant impact on energy or latency.
This enables numerical accuracy, particularly important for operations sensitive to precision loss such as attention.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p10" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p10.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.p10.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">Stream Decoder: </span>
To reduce latency and storage overhead, weight tiles are stored in compressed block formats in memory and transferred on-chip to the memory buffer by the memory DMA engine.
Next, the compute DMA streams compressed weights into the <span id="S5.p10.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Stream Decoder</span>, which performs on-the-fly dequantization, converting block-quantized values into standard BF16.
This continues until a full batch of 64 BF16 values is reconstructed, corresponding to a single weight tile.
Once dequantized, the tile is broadcast across all active tile multipliers within the core via a 1024-bit wide compute bus.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p11" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p11.1" class="ltx_p">Our stream decoder supports on-the-fly dequantization of multiple formats, including BFP <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib69" title="" class="ltx_ref">53</a>]</cite>, MxFP <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">9</a>]</cite>, and NxFP <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib71" title="" class="ltx_ref">36</a>]</cite>, with configurable bitwidths ranging from 4 to 8 bits.
This flexibility allows us to efficiently compress weights off-chip while preserving the ability to compute at full precision on-chip, minimizing off-chip capacity and energy without compromising accuracy.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.F8" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1"><img src="2602.18568v1/exe-timeline-llama3-8b-bs-1-chiplets-64-seq-16k.png" id="S5.F8.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/153;" width="476" height="153" alt="Refer to caption"></div><div class="ltx_flex_break"></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1"><img src="2602.18568v1/exe-timeline-llama3-8b-bs-32-chiplets-64-seq-8k.png" id="S5.F8.g2" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/153;" width="476" height="153" alt="Refer to caption"></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Fig. 8: </span>Simulation of one CU in a 64-CU system running Llama3-8B.
Top: Batch size 1, seq len 16k. Bottom: Batch size 32, seq len 8k.
Each timeline shows memory, compute, and network utilization, buffer usage, and power. Memory power dominates total system power, highlighting the RPU’s unique power provisioning.
The plot also shows that batch size 32 generates tokens <math id="S5.F8.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>13× slower than batch size 1, primarily due to sequential KV$ computations.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">VI </span><span id="S6.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">RPU Software Stack and Simulation</span></h2>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">RPU ISA and Compiler: </span> The RPU software stack provides a deterministic compilation flow from PyTorch graphs to hardware execution.
The RPU ISA hardens optimized vector-matrix and elementwise dataflows directly into hardware, exposing each as a single CISC-style instruction.
Each instruction specifies operand addresses, tensor dimensions, and data types, while the hardware executes a fixed streaming schedule with near-roofline utilization.
Computation follows a <span id="S6.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">push-based</span> dataflow: DMA engines deterministically inject data into buffers, and pipelines advance when inputs are ready.
Hardware-managed pipeline arbiter flags are embedded within each instruction to synchronize compute, memory, and network pipelines, eliminating the need for software polling and ensuring deadlock-free progress.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p2.1" class="ltx_p">A lightweight Python compiler traces PyTorch operations and lowers them to RPU primitives.
For example, a <span id="S6.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">torch.nn.Linear</span> layer compiles into a three-stage microkernel – Loading, Looping, and Launching – that programs DMAs, drives the VMM pipeline, and forwards activations, respectively.
The compiler statically orders all DMA and compute instructions, pre-shards and quantizes weights, and generates synchronized instruction streams for the memory, compute, and network pipelines.
Together, the ISA and compiler form a compact, deterministic toolchain that provides predictable, near-roofline performance for token generation.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">Deployment: </span>
Each RPU core includes a lightweight instruction-fetch pipeline that executes a small set of long-running instructions for a full LLM.
This enables fully autonomous execution, eliminating the host-driven offload model used by GPUs.
The host processor performs only coordination tasks such as transferring KV$ from the prefill engine into RPU memory.
After each transformer layer, the RPU triggers an interrupt to the host and reports generated tokens or completed queries and returns the corresponding KV caches.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">RTL Simulations: </span>
We implement a proof-of-concept RPU in SystemC using Catapult HLS <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib57" title="" class="ltx_ref">62</a>, <a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">69</a>]</cite>, targeting TSMC N16 and projecting to N2 using published scaling factors <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib66" title="" class="ltx_ref">59</a>, <a href="#bib.bib64" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>, <a href="#bib.bib65" title="" class="ltx_ref">60</a>]</cite>.
RTL simulation includes a single-core CU, multi-CU packaging, and board-level integration.
Key microkernels (e.g., VMM, DMA) are synthesized using VCS, Design Compiler, and PowerPro to extract calibrated energy and area.
SRAM and interconnect energy are modeled analytically, and memory energy is provided by our HBM-CO analytical model, which captures the energy and bandwidth tradeoffs of capacity-optimized memory devices.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Compiled PyTorch transformer layers were executed on the RTL model to verify functional correctness and dataflow behavior.
However, full-system cycle-accurate simulation remains computationally intensive: simulating a <span id="S6.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">2k × 2k</span> VMM on a 4-core RPU requires approximately 6.5 minutes, making end-to-end design space exploration (DSE) for LLM inference impractical at the RTL level.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p6.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">Event Driven Simulation: </span>
To address RTL simulation latency, we developed a higher-level event-driven simulator that reproduces the behavior of the RTL model using symbolic transactions that capture address, size, and type instead of real tensor data.
The simulator models all key microarchitectural events – data transfers, stalls, and arbitration – using parameters calibrated to RTL throughput, bandwidth, and latency.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p7.1" class="ltx_p">The event-driven simulator runs orders of magnitude faster than RTL while matching its latency and power estimates.
It supports full-model DSE across models, batch sizes, sequence lengths, memory devices, and scales of deployments, while exposing transient behaviors such as buffer occupancy, pipeline stalls, and synchronization delays (Figure <a href="#S5.F8" title="Fig. 8 ‣ V Micro-Architecture ‣ RPU – A Reasoning Processing Unit" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a>).
The simulator also serves as a debugging and validation tool: violations of data dependencies appear as execution stalls, allowing developers to visually trace and correct synchronization issues in the simulation framework prior to deployment.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p8.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.p8.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">Simulation Results: </span>
Figure <a href="#S5.F8" title="Fig. 8 ‣ V Micro-Architecture ‣ RPU – A Reasoning Processing Unit" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a> shows a simulation of the first transformer layers in Llama3-8B on a 64-CU RPU using the candidate HBM-CO from Section <a href="#S3" title="III Capacity Optimized High Bandwidth Memory ‣ RPU – A Reasoning Processing Unit" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">III</span></a>.
We compare batch sizes 1 and 32, breaking down execution across memory, compute, and network pipelines, along with buffer and power traces. Each row represents a single CU, with red lines indicating average utilization per kernel.
We highlight instances where the RPU’s decoupled pipelines enable out-of-order execution between memory, compute, and communication to unlock behaviors that conventional architectures cannot exploit.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p9" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p9.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.p9.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">Batch Size 1: </span>
<span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="S6.p9.pic1" class="ltx_picture" height="15.45" overflow="visible" style="vertical-align:-3.71px" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 15.45 15.45" width="15.45"><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="0.4pt" transform="translate(0,15.45) matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 0) translate(7.72,0) translate(0,7.72)"><path style="fill:none" d="M 7.45 0 C 7.45 4.11 4.11 7.45 0 7.45 C -4.11 7.45 -7.45 4.11 -7.45 0 C -7.45 -4.11 -4.11 -7.45 0 -7.45 C 4.11 -7.45 7.45 -4.11 7.45 0 Z M 0 0"></path><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 -3.2 -4.01)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:0.5em;--ltx-fo-height:0.63em;--ltx-fo-depth:0em;font-size:9.25pt;" height="8.03" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 8.03)" width="6.4"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content"><span id="S6.p9.pic1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">1</span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span>
During the first VMM (<span id="S6.p9.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">wQKV</span>) execution is bounded by network-latency to broadcast activations across all CUs.
This is reflected in the timeline by low network bandwidth utilization, and early memory-pipeline completion.
Traditional architectures would stall the memory; however, the decoupled memory pipeline enables the RPU to simply continue fetching weights from memory to the on-chip buffer, while the compute pipeline lags the memory stream by <math id="S6.p9.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>80kB waiting for activations to arrive from the network.
During this period, power consumption is dominated by reading weights from memory: <math id="S6.p9.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>6.7W at full BW / CU (<span id="S6.p9.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">512 GB/sec</span>) and <math id="S6.p9.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>1.7pJ/b datapath to write to the memory-buffer.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p10" class="ltx_para"><span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="S6.p10.pic1" class="ltx_picture" height="15.45" overflow="visible" style="vertical-align:-3.71px" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 15.45 15.45" width="15.45"><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="0.4pt" transform="translate(0,15.45) matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 0) translate(7.72,0) translate(0,7.72)"><path style="fill:none" d="M 7.45 0 C 7.45 4.11 4.11 7.45 0 7.45 C -4.11 7.45 -7.45 4.11 -7.45 0 C -7.45 -4.11 -4.11 -7.45 0 -7.45 C 4.11 -7.45 7.45 -4.11 7.45 0 Z M 0 0"></path><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 -3.2 -4.01)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:0.5em;--ltx-fo-height:0.63em;--ltx-fo-depth:0em;font-size:9.25pt;" height="8.03" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 8.03)" width="6.4"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content"><span id="S6.p10.pic1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">2</span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span>
<p id="S6.p10.1" class="ltx_p">Prior to the <span id="S6.p10.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">QK<sup id="S6.p10.1.1.1" class="ltx_sup">⊤</sup></span> computation, compute stalls as each CU gathers its shard of the <span id="S6.p10.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Q</span>, <span id="S6.p10.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">K</span>, and <span id="S6.p10.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">V</span> vectors – 32 <span id="S6.p10.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Q</span> heads and 8 <span id="S6.p10.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">KV</span> heads distributed across 64 CUs means each <span id="S6.p10.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Q</span>-vector spans two CUs while <span id="S6.p10.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">KV</span>-vectors span eight CUs.
Similarly, during <span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="S6.p10.pic2" class="ltx_picture" height="15.45" overflow="visible" style="vertical-align:-3.71px" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 15.45 15.45" width="15.45"><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="0.4pt" transform="translate(0,15.45) matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 0) translate(7.72,0) translate(0,7.72)"><path style="fill:none" d="M 7.45 0 C 7.45 4.11 4.11 7.45 0 7.45 C -4.11 7.45 -7.45 4.11 -7.45 0 C -7.45 -4.11 -4.11 -7.45 0 -7.45 C 4.11 -7.45 7.45 -4.11 7.45 0 Z M 0 0"></path><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 -3.2 -4.01)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:0.5em;--ltx-fo-height:0.63em;--ltx-fo-depth:0em;font-size:9.25pt;" height="8.03" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 8.03)" width="6.4"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content"><span id="S6.p10.pic2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">4</span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span>, the compute stalls waiting first for a distributed <span id="S6.p10.1.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">max</span> collective to calculate <span id="S6.p10.1.10" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">softmax</span>, then an <span id="S6.p10.1.11" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">exp-sum</span> reduction across the CUs sharing the 8 GQA-heads.
These examples of cross-CU synchronization and network delays stall the compute pipeline, while the memory pipeline continues to prefetch and move weights and <span id="S6.p10.1.12" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">KV$</span> to the on-chip buffer.
These types of network latency-bound periods are common in tensor-parallel distributed systems, where latency-bound network collectives are often on the orders of <math id="S6.p10.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>μ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu</annotation></semantics></math>seconds, leading to periods of fully stalled execution.
The RPU allows the memory pipeline to continue prefetching ahead of the compute stream, effectively eliminating any incurred network collective overheads.</p>
</div>
