<div id="S6.p11" class="ltx_para"><span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="S6.p11.pic1" class="ltx_picture" height="15.45" overflow="visible" style="vertical-align:-3.71px" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 15.45 15.45" width="15.45"><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="0.4pt" transform="translate(0,15.45) matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 0) translate(7.72,0) translate(0,7.72)"><path style="fill:none" d="M 7.45 0 C 7.45 4.11 4.11 7.45 0 7.45 C -4.11 7.45 -7.45 4.11 -7.45 0 C -7.45 -4.11 -4.11 -7.45 0 -7.45 C 4.11 -7.45 7.45 -4.11 7.45 0 Z M 0 0"></path><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 -3.2 -4.01)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:0.5em;--ltx-fo-height:0.63em;--ltx-fo-depth:0em;font-size:9.25pt;" height="8.03" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 8.03)" width="6.4"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content"><span id="S6.p11.pic1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">3</span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span>
<p id="S6.p11.1" class="ltx_p">During the <span id="S6.p11.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">QK<sup id="S6.p11.1.1.1" class="ltx_sup">⊤</sup></span> computation, each <span id="S6.p11.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Q</span>-vector (4 per GQA head) is assigned to a TMAC, while prefetched <span id="S6.p11.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">K$</span> entries are broadcast from the memory buffer.
Similarly, in <span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="S6.p11.pic2" class="ltx_picture" height="15.45" overflow="visible" style="vertical-align:-3.71px" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 15.45 15.45" width="15.45"><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="0.4pt" transform="translate(0,15.45) matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 0) translate(7.72,0) translate(0,7.72)"><path style="fill:none" d="M 7.45 0 C 7.45 4.11 4.11 7.45 0 7.45 C -4.11 7.45 -7.45 4.11 -7.45 0 C -7.45 -4.11 -4.11 -7.45 0 -7.45 C 4.11 -7.45 7.45 -4.11 7.45 0 Z M 0 0"></path><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 -3.2 -4.01)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:0.5em;--ltx-fo-height:0.63em;--ltx-fo-depth:0em;font-size:9.25pt;" height="8.03" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 8.03)" width="6.4"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content"><span id="S6.p11.pic2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">5</span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span> the <span id="S6.p11.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">wUp/wGate</span> phase drives compute to full utilization while processing the accumulated weights.
This is a unique opportunistic moment for the RPU, as decoupled pipelines enabled the memory-bandwidth to stay fully saturated throughout network delays and compute stalls.
Later, this enables the compute to play “catch-up” until all the available data is consumed from the on-chip buffer, returning to the memory-bandwidth bound performance.
Power during this period rises due to higher compute utilization, from <math id="S6.p11.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>1.5W to <math id="S6.p11.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>5W per CU, reflecting full datapath activity.
Once the buffer is drained, compute utilization returns to the memory-bound performance.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p12" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p12.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.p12.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">Batch Size 32: </span>
<span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="S6.p12.pic1" class="ltx_picture" height="15.45" overflow="visible" style="vertical-align:-3.71px" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 15.45 15.45" width="15.45"><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="0.4pt" transform="translate(0,15.45) matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 0) translate(7.72,0) translate(0,7.72)"><path style="fill:none" d="M 7.45 0 C 7.45 4.11 4.11 7.45 0 7.45 C -4.11 7.45 -7.45 4.11 -7.45 0 C -7.45 -4.11 -4.11 -7.45 0 -7.45 C 4.11 -7.45 7.45 -4.11 7.45 0 Z M 0 0"></path><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 -3.2 -4.01)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:0.5em;--ltx-fo-height:0.63em;--ltx-fo-depth:0em;font-size:9.25pt;" height="8.03" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 8.03)" width="6.4"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content"><span id="S6.p12.pic1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">1</span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span>
With a larger batch size, weight matrix operations become compute-bound.
Specifically, during <span id="S6.p12.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">wUp/wGate</span>, weight are read from memory in <math id="S6.p12.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>2<math id="S6.p12.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>μ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu</annotation></semantics></math>s, while compute is <math id="S6.p12.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>4x longer.
While the RPU is compute-bound operating on the <span id="S6.p12.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">wUp/wGate</span> computation, the memory pipeline prefetches ahead, streaming in <span id="S6.p12.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">KV$</span> and filling each CU’s buffer with <math id="S6.p12.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>6MB of weights totaling <math id="S6.p12.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>384MB system-wide.
This lookahead window is beyond the capabilities of GPU architectures like H100, which lack both the on-chip capacity and pipeline decoupling to absorb such deep prefetching.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p13" class="ltx_para"><span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="S6.p13.pic1" class="ltx_picture" height="15.45" overflow="visible" style="vertical-align:-3.71px" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 15.45 15.45" width="15.45"><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="0.4pt" transform="translate(0,15.45) matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 0) translate(7.72,0) translate(0,7.72)"><path style="fill:none" d="M 7.45 0 C 7.45 4.11 4.11 7.45 0 7.45 C -4.11 7.45 -7.45 4.11 -7.45 0 C -7.45 -4.11 -4.11 -7.45 0 -7.45 C 4.11 -7.45 7.45 -4.11 7.45 0 Z M 0 0"></path><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 -3.2 -4.01)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:0.5em;--ltx-fo-height:0.63em;--ltx-fo-depth:0em;font-size:9.25pt;" height="8.03" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 8.03)" width="6.4"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content"><span id="S6.p13.pic1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">2</span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span>
<p id="S6.p13.1" class="ltx_p">After a sequence of compute-bound weight matrix multiplications, the attention computation begins, entering a <span id="S6.p13.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">KV$</span>-intensive phase.
Unlike weights, <span id="S6.p13.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">KV$</span> entries are query-unique, offering reuse only among GQA heads.
Thus, this phase is inherently memory-bandwidth-bound.
However, <span id="S6.p13.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">KV$</span> has already been prefetched on-chip which allows the system to stream <span id="S6.p13.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">KV$</span> directly from the on-chip buffer and operate at a compute-bound performance.
As a result, the buffer drains rapidly, as the compute “catches-up” to the memory stream.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p14" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p14.1" class="ltx_p">A batched LLM decode system naturally alternates between compute-bound weight layers and memory-bound <span id="S6.p14.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">KV$</span> layers, leading to pipeline underutilization on traditional architectures.
Our design breaks this limitation by <span id="S6.p14.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">smoothing out the bimodal workload</span> (compute-bound weights vs memory-bound <span id="S6.p14.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">KV$</span>) and <span id="S6.p14.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">absorbing phase-imbalance into the memory buffer</span>, letting decoupled pipelines handle them independently.
By smoothing performance across layers, we enable sustained utilization of both memory and compute.
Without this buffering strategy, overall latency would increase by up to 1.6×.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p15" class="ltx_para"><span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="S6.p15.pic1" class="ltx_picture" height="15.45" overflow="visible" style="vertical-align:-3.71px" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 15.45 15.45" width="15.45"><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="0.4pt" transform="translate(0,15.45) matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 0) translate(7.72,0) translate(0,7.72)"><path style="fill:none" d="M 7.45 0 C 7.45 4.11 4.11 7.45 0 7.45 C -4.11 7.45 -7.45 4.11 -7.45 0 C -7.45 -4.11 -4.11 -7.45 0 -7.45 C 4.11 -7.45 7.45 -4.11 7.45 0 Z M 0 0"></path><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 -3.2 -4.01)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:0.5em;--ltx-fo-height:0.63em;--ltx-fo-depth:0em;font-size:9.25pt;" height="8.03" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 8.03)" width="6.4"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content"><span id="S6.p15.pic1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">3</span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span>
<p id="S6.p15.1" class="ltx_p">Once the buffer is drained, compute returns to the memory-bound performance and power drop accordingly, marking the end of the amortization window.
Larger batch sizes allow deeper prefetching, leading to a tradeoff in sequence length versus batch size to fully saturate bandwidth.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S6.F9" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18568v1/energy_vs_capacity_llama3-405b.svg" id="S6.F9.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/320;" width="476" height="320"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Fig. 9: </span>Pareto frontier of HBM-CO memories for Llama3-405B inference on 64-CU RPU, annotated by stepwise changes in optimal HBM-CO.
These represent the set of HBM-CO chiplets useful for a memory-chiplet ecosystem.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S7" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">VII </span><span id="S7.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">System Implications of HBM-CO</span></h2>

<div id="S7.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">HBM-CO memories improve efficiency at the device level, but their true benefits emerge only through full-system evaluation.
Figure <a href="#S6.F9" title="Fig. 9 ‣ VI RPU Software Stack and Simulation ‣ RPU – A Reasoning Processing Unit" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a> shows energy per inference (y-axis) versus system memory capacity for a 64-CU RPU.
HBM-CO memory configurations form a Pareto frontier showing the energy-capacity tradeoff; non-optimal points are omitted for clarity.
Capacity reductions are progressively applied to an HBM3e-like memory to traverse the Pareto frontier.
The best capacity reduction strategy is annotated between configurations.
The optimal HBM-CO has the smallest device capacity that meets the system-level requirement to store the target model.</p>
</div>
<div id="S7.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For a 64-CU RPU running Llama3-405B with a single query and an 8k sequence length, the optimal HBM-CO configuration has a memory capacity of 192 MB per core.
Compared to HBM3e, HBM-CO reduces the energy per bit by 2× from the memory cell to the IO, while at the system-level the energy per inference improves by 1.7× due to memory dominating the energy consumption.
A similar tradeoff exists for system cost.
Despite a 1.6× higher cost per GB, reduced capacity HBM-CO yields a 5.2× decrease in per-device cost, translating to a 4.3× total system cost reduction when factoring in compute, interposer, and substrate.</p>
</div>
<div id="S7.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.p3.1" class="ltx_p">As illustrated in Figure <a href="#S6.F9" title="Fig. 9 ‣ VI RPU Software Stack and Simulation ‣ RPU – A Reasoning Processing Unit" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a>, several HBM-CO configurations offer even lower energy per inference but remain inaccessible at the current 64-CU scale due to their limited memory capacity.
Unlocking these more energy-efficient memories requires increasing the number of CUs, thereby decreasing the required memory per CU.</p>
</div>
<div id="S7.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.p4.1" class="ltx_p">A key goal in deploying the RPU is to maintain workload flexibility without proliferating hardware SKUs.
In the emerging chiplet ecosystem, the HBM-CO designs along the Pareto frontier of Figure <a href="#S6.F9" title="Fig. 9 ‣ VI RPU Software Stack and Simulation ‣ RPU – A Reasoning Processing Unit" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a> are sufficient to cover the useful BW/Cap design space.
These chiplets can be mixed and matched at the package level to enable design customizations without fabricating a new ASIC.
Figure <a href="#S7.F10" title="Fig. 10 ‣ VII System Implications of HBM-CO ‣ RPU – A Reasoning Processing Unit" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a> extends this idea by showing how to select among these variants for a given workload.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S7.F10" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18568v1/batch_vs_seq_bwcap_and_slowdown.png" id="S7.F10.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:476/555;" width="476" height="555" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Fig. 10: </span>
RPU with 64 CUs running Llama4-Maverick showing batch size versus sequence length, comparing optimal HBM-CO BW/Cap and slowdown relative to BS=1, Seq Len=8K. Slowdown sub-metrics indicate the fraction of capacity used for KV cache versus active parameters and total capacity.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S7.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S7.F10" title="Fig. 10 ‣ VII System Implications of HBM-CO ‣ RPU – A Reasoning Processing Unit" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a> (top) is an HBM-CO SKU selection map for a 64-CU RPU running Llama4-Maverick.
Each memory chiplet has a fixed bandwidth interface, resulting in a total system bandwidth of 32 TB/s.
Given this fixed bandwidth, system capacity is optimized by selecting the most efficient HBM-CO chiplet configuration from Figure <a href="#S6.F9" title="Fig. 9 ‣ VI RPU Software Stack and Simulation ‣ RPU – A Reasoning Processing Unit" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a>, to minimize both energy per inference and overall cost while satisfying capacity for each batch size and sequence length combination.</p>
</div>
<div id="S7.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.p6.1" class="ltx_p">High BW/Cap SKUs maximize efficiency but limit the range of supported batch and sequence lengths, while lower BW/Cap SKUs trade some efficiency for broader capacity coverage.
Importantly, Figure <a href="#S7.F10" title="Fig. 10 ‣ VII System Implications of HBM-CO ‣ RPU – A Reasoning Processing Unit" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a> (top) shows that high-BW/Cap memories (5-6x HBM3e) are better suited for long-context, low-batch inference, which underscores the capacity overprovisioning of using off-the-shelf HBM3e.
Increasing the number of CUs raises the optimal BW/Cap, enhancing efficiency at scale.</p>
</div>
<div id="S7.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.p7.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S7.F10" title="Fig. 10 ‣ VII System Implications of HBM-CO ‣ RPU – A Reasoning Processing Unit" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a> (bottom) quantifies how batching and sequence length impact latency.
As batch size or sequence length increase, the per-query token generation latency increases.
This is illustrated by tools such as InferenceMax <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">56</a>]</cite>, highlighting that low-batch inference is key for low latency.
Longer sequences also intensify bandwidth pressure during attention – more than 50% of the active parameters are KV$ for BS=8 128k.
Therefore, the relative efficiency gap between the RPU and conventional GPUs widens due to the RPU’s bandwidth advantage, underscoring its use for long-context, low-latency inference.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S8" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">VIII </span><span id="S8.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Strong Scaling Analysis</span></h2>

<div id="S8.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S8.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S8.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">Strong Scaling Analysis: </span>
We conduct a strong-scaling study by varying the number of CUs.
Speedup is reported relative to the smallest configuration capable of fitting each model.
Figure <a href="#S8.F11" title="Fig. 11 ‣ VIII Strong Scaling Analysis ‣ RPU – A Reasoning Processing Unit" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a> shows results for Llama models, compared against an NVIDIA H100 at ISO TDP using the methodology from Section <a href="#S2" title="II Motivation for a Decode-Optimized System ‣ RPU – A Reasoning Processing Unit" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">II</span></a> with 4-bit weights and 16-bit activations <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>]</cite> and full tensor-parallelism.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S8.F11" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18568v1/strong_scaling_comparison.svg" id="S8.F11.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:452/194;" width="452" height="194"></object></div><div class="ltx_flex_break"></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18568v1/latency_and_bw_utilization.svg" id="S8.F11.g2" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:452/194;" width="452" height="194"></object></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Fig. 11: </span>Top: Strong scaling for Llama models under ISO TDP vs H100. Bottom: Output tokens per second per query (8xH200 from <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>]</cite>) and bandwidth utilization versus batch size.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S8.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S8.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S8.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">Batch Size 1 – Fastest Thinking Speed: </span>
Batch size 1 represents the fastest possible “thinking speed” of a model.
At ISO TDP, the RPU significantly outperforms H100 inference.
Notably, the RPU latency is 47.0× faster than a 2xH100 at 1400W TDP for Llama3-70B and 45.3× faster than a 4×H100 at 2800W TDP for Llama3-405B.
The 405B example is illustrated in Figure <a href="#S8.F11" title="Fig. 11 ‣ VIII Strong Scaling Analysis ‣ RPU – A Reasoning Processing Unit" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a> (top) by the orange diamond (4xH100s) aligned to a 308 CU RPU system at ISO TDP.</p>
</div>
<div id="S8.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S8.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Even more compelling is the peak performance of the RPU, achieved by scaling to the optimal number of CUs for each model:
Llama3-70B at 204 CUs achieves 0.4 ms/token, and
Llama3-405B at 428 CUs achieves 1.0 ms/token.
Llama4-Maverick at 128 CUs achieves 0.2 ms/token.
These are the fastest token generation latencies reported to date for these models.
<span id="S8.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Notably, we are the first system capable of sustaining over 200 TB/s of tensor-parallel memory bandwidth during inference for a 405B parameter model.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S8.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S8.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Beyond these scales, performance plateaus as broadcasting the activation becomes the bottleneck.
To overcome this limit, we propose two future directions:
1) Reduce on-chip forwarding latency.
2) Reduces hop count by adding another level of scale-out to Figure <a href="#S3.F6" title="Fig. 6 ‣ III Capacity Optimized High Bandwidth Memory ‣ RPU – A Reasoning Processing Unit" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> which interconnects ring-stations.</p>
</div>
<div id="S8.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S8.p5.1" class="ltx_p">An important insight from this study is that memory customization enables model- and deployment-specific system design.
For instance, an RPU designed for the high-performance edge running Llama3-70B achieves 3.5ms/token using a memory configuration with BW/Cap=227 at 220W TDP.
Separately, an edge-optimized system for Llama4-Maverick achieves 1.1ms/token at BW/Cap=38 (comparable to HBM3e) and 260W TDP.
In contrast, for datacenter-scale deployments targeting 1kW TDP, we design an RPU for Llama3-70B with more CUs that achieves 0.65ms/token with a BW/Cap of 682 (the highest in our design space) while a datacenter RPU for Llama4-Maverick reaches 0.24ms/token at BW/Cap=170.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S8.F12" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18568v1/llama3_405B_energy_analysis.svg" id="S8.F12.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/278;" width="476" height="278"></object></div><div class="ltx_flex_break"></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18568v1/llama3_405B_cost_analysis.svg" id="S8.F12.g2" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/278;" width="476" height="278"></object></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Fig. 12: </span>Energy and cost analysis for scales of CUs running Llama3-405B at batch size 1. Top: Energy per inference and optimal memory selection. Bottom: Normalized system cost.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S8.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S8.p6.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S8.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">Batched Inference on the RPU:</span>
Figure <a href="#S8.F11" title="Fig. 11 ‣ VIII Strong Scaling Analysis ‣ RPU – A Reasoning Processing Unit" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a> (bottom left) compares output tokens/sec per query across Llama models using a 128 CU RPU and an 8×H200 baseline reported by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>]</cite>.
Llama4-Scout achieves the highest throughput across all batch sizes, closely followed by Llama4-Maverick.
Activating more unique experts in Maverick reduces per-expert parallelism, leading to a 1.2-1.3× decrease in performance compared to Scout’s 16-expert configuration.</p>
</div>
<div id="S8.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S8.p7.1" class="ltx_p">As batch size increases, per-query throughput decreases primarily due to serialized KV cache computations.
Figure <a href="#S8.F11" title="Fig. 11 ‣ VIII Strong Scaling Analysis ‣ RPU – A Reasoning Processing Unit" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a> (bottom right) demonstrates this behavior, indicating all models operate in a memory bandwidth-bound regime up to a batch size of 8.
Beyond this point, the Llama3-405B model becomes compute-bound, as its attention mechanism features a high arithmetic intensity (16 queries per KV head), saturating available compute resources.</p>
</div>
<div id="S8.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S8.p8.1" class="ltx_p">In contrast, the Llama4 models maintain high memory bandwidth utilization (above 80%) up to batch size 128.
Their attention design, with only 5 queries per KV head, and MoE structure, are low per-token arithmetic intensity.
Our layer smoothing technique balances arithmetic intensity across compute-bound layers (e.g., shared projections and MLP layers) and memory-bound layers (e.g., attention and MoE layers).
Between the two Llama4 variants, Scout becomes compute-bound earlier due to heavier per-expert loads (only 16 experts) versus Maverick’s 128-expert setup distributes tokens across more experts, preserving memory-bandwidth demands.</p>
</div>
<div id="S8.p9" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S8.p9.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S8.p9.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">Energy and Cost Analysis: </span>
Figure <a href="#S8.F12" title="Fig. 12 ‣ VIII Strong Scaling Analysis ‣ RPU – A Reasoning Processing Unit" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">12</span></a> (top) extends our strong scaling results by analyzing energy per inference for Llama3-405B at batch size 1.
The majority of the energy is consumed by memory accesses, making memory selection a dominant factor in system efficiency.
To minimize energy, we explore HBM-CO design points along the Pareto frontier (Section <a href="#S7" title="VII System Implications of HBM-CO ‣ RPU – A Reasoning Processing Unit" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">VII</span></a>), selecting the BW/Cap ratio that best matches system scale and capacity requirements.</p>
</div>
<div id="S8.p10" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S8.p10.1" class="ltx_p">At smaller scales, lower BW/Cap memory modules are required to meet overall capacity needs, resulting in higher energy per inference.
As the system scale increases, each CU stores a smaller fraction of the model, allowing for a higher BW/Cap memory with lower capacity and improved energy efficiency.
Energy per inference improves steadily with scale until 268 CUs where the highest BW/Cap memory module in the design space is selected.</p>
</div>
<div id="S8.p11" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S8.p11.1" class="ltx_p">Compared to an HBM3e BW/Cap memory, the HBM-CO memory improves energy efficiency by up to 2.2×.
Similarly, compared to a 4×H100 system running Llama3-405B, the HBM-CO optimized configuration achieves 6.5× lower energy per inference.
Combined with the latency-optimized design point at 428 CUs, this translates to a 412× improvement in energy-delay product (EDP) relative to the 4×H100 baseline.
This highlights the power of co-designing memory and compute around bandwidth per capacity to unlock both latency and efficiency at scale.</p>
</div>
<div id="S8.p12" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S8.p12.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S8.F12" title="Fig. 12 ‣ VIII Strong Scaling Analysis ‣ RPU – A Reasoning Processing Unit" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">12</span></a> (bottom) shows the normalized total system cost broken down by silicon, memory, substrate, and PCB.
Costs are normalized to the smallest valid configuration for Llama3-405B.
As expected, compute cost grows linearly with CU count, while memory cost increases sublinearly due to adaptive HBM-CO selection.
At each scale, the memory configuration is selected from the HBM-CO Pareto frontier using the highest BW/cap memory which satisfies the required capacity.
Discrete jumps visible in the memory cost curve correspond to transitions between HBM-CO tiers.
While high BW/Cap memories are more expensive per GB, they eliminate capacity over-provision.
As a result, total system cost is reduced.</p>
</div>
<div id="S8.p13" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S8.p13.1" class="ltx_p">Compared to using a fixed HBM3e memory, the HBM-CO system reduces total cost by up to 12.4×.
At scale, its memory-to-compute cost ratio matches that of an 8×H100 DGX <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>]</cite>, demonstrating that HBM-CO enable efficient bandwidth scaling while keeping costs reasonable.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S8.F13" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18568v1/speedup_and_edp_vs_h100.svg" id="S8.F13.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/179;" width="476" height="179"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Fig. 13: </span>Speedup and energy-per-inference of an RPU versus and H100, sweeping batch size for Llama models with 8k prefill 2k decode.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S8.p14" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S8.p14.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S8.p14.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">Energy per Inference versus Batch Size: </span>
Figure <a href="#S8.F13" title="Fig. 13 ‣ VIII Strong Scaling Analysis ‣ RPU – A Reasoning Processing Unit" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">13</span></a> shows speedup and energy-per-inference of the RPU over an H100 across batch sizes for Llama3-8B and Llama3-70B.
Larger batch sizes improve the GPU’s compute efficiency.
However, concurrent queries inflate the KV$ cache latency, introducing phase imbalance that the GPU cannot hide.
For the RPU, small 4k sequences limit the benefit of decoupled pipelines because weight computation dominates, leaving less room to overlap KV$ prefetching.
As a result, performance gains plateau at <math id="S8.p14.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>15-20× over the H100, though the RPU still maintains higher throughput and better energy efficiency.</p>
</div>
<div id="S8.p15" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S8.p15.1" class="ltx_p">At small batch sizes, the RPU shines, delivering over 40-50× speedup and 8-10x energy-per-inference, driven by its higher memory bandwidth and ability to efficiently execute small kernels with minimal synchronization overhead.
In contrast, H100 performance performs poorly in this regime, as it is significantly bandwidth-bound and suffers from kernel launch and scheduling overheads.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S9" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">IX </span><span id="S9.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Decomposed Contributions</span></h2>

<div id="S9.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S9.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S9.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Contribution 1 – HBM-CO Memory: </span>
Compared to an RPU system using HBM3e, HBM-CO offers up to 2.2× lower energy per inference and 12.4× lower system cost, primarily by eliminating excess capacity and reducing internal wire lengths.
These savings allow us to scale the number of compute units at ISO-TDP, leading to a 2.1× latency improvement.</p>
</div>
<div id="S9.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S9.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S9.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Contribution 2 – RPU Power and Area Provisioning:</span>
By rebalancing the compute-to-bandwidth ratio relative to an RPU provisioned like an H100 (<math id="S9.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>200 Ops/Byte), the RPU saves 3.3× die cost and 2.6× TDP utilization, leading to a 2.2× latency improvement when scaling out at ISO-TDP.</p>
</div>
<div id="S9.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S9.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S9.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Contribution 3 – Microarchitectural Decoupling: </span>
Fine-grained network sharding eliminates global synchronization, avoiding up to a 2.0× latency penalty from collective stalls.
Memory-compute decoupling enables deep prefetching, preventing a 1.2× slowdown from serialized kernel execution.
In batch size 32 workloads, decoupled execution allows the RPU to straddle the roofline across memory-bound (SDPA, MoE) and compute-bound (Linear) kernels, improving latency by up to 1.6×.
These changes also improve energy efficiency: 1.4× over a monolithic NUMA-style baseline via shorter data paths, and 1.7× at the SRAM interface through on-the-fly stream dequantization.
Together, these energy efficiency gains enable the system to scale to 2.4× more bandwidth at ISO-TDP.</p>
</div>
<div id="S9.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S9.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S9.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Cumulative Performance:</span>
HBM-CO, aligned provisioning, and decoupled pipelines enable 20-40× higher effective memory bandwidth at ISO-TDP, consistent with simulation results.</p>
</div>
<div id="S9.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S9.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S9.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">RPU Application Domain: </span>
Human-computer interaction literature identifies an interaction-latency threshold on the order of ten seconds, beyond which working memory decays and users are likely to context-switch, incurring re-orientation overheads <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">42</a>, <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">39</a>, <a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">15</a>]</cite>.
Accordingly, reasoning systems must minimize end-to-end latency to preserve turn-taking and cognitive continuity, rather than maximizing throughput.
This captures the motivation behind the RPU: we want advanced intelligence at our fingertips.
The RPU targets these reasoning-intensive, interactive workloads requiring end-to-end responses such as multi-step planning, problem solving, iterative coding, and writing assistance, which currently take tens of seconds to minutes on today’s systems <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">56</a>]</cite>.
By exploiting the latency benefits of low-batch inference, it delivers state-of-the-art responsiveness and per-query performance.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S10" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">X </span><span id="S10.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Related Work</span></h2>

<div id="S10.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S10.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S10.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">DRAM-Centric General-Purpose Accelerators: </span>
Systems such as NVIDIA H100 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>]</cite>, AMD MI300x <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">61</a>]</cite>, SambaNova <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">52</a>]</cite>, and TPU <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">23</a>]</cite> use high-capacity HBM, large shared caches, and dense compute to support both training and inference.
These architectures typically feature a single NUMA domain with distributed controllers and centralized caches.
While this enables flexible data access, it creates long memory paths and high energy per access, which is especially harmful for memory-bound decode.
In contrast, the RPU uses a fine-grained NUMA design where each core has its own HBM-CO DRAM channel and local SRAM buffer, eliminating shared caches and reducing on-chip data movement.
This decouples compute, memory, and network pipelines, sustaining high bandwidth utilization.</p>
</div>
<div id="S10.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S10.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S10.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">SRAM-Centric Custom Accelerators: </span>
Custom accelerators such as Groq <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>]</cite>, Cerebras WSE-3 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">64</a>]</cite>, and Graphcore IPU <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">29</a>]</cite> rely on SRAM as main memory.
However, the limited density of SRAM makes it impractical to store large models efficiently.
For example, a 70B parameter model deployed on Groq requires hundreds of accelerator cards, while Cerebras spans four wafer-scale chips.</p>
</div>
<div id="S10.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S10.p3.1" class="ltx_p">To utilize their full SRAM bandwidth, these systems shard each matrix across a large compute fabric.
For example, Cerebras may distribute a single VMM across 900,000 cores, requiring vector broadcasts to traverse up to 1,000 core-to-core hops and reductions to span the entire wafer.
With the model globally distributed, network communication, not compute or memory access, becomes the primary performance bottleneck due to SRAM’s low density.
In contrast, each RPU reasoning core is significantly more capable than the ultra-lightweight cores used in Groq or Cerebras, with higher FLOP throughput and wider data buses.
As a result, more of the workload is processed locally per core, reducing reliance on multi-hop communication.
Additionally, the RPU’s hierarchical ring network has a much smaller diameter than mesh or wafer-scale fabrics, further minimizing the number of hops required for vector broadcasts and reductions.</p>
</div>
<div id="S10.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S10.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S10.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">Processing In Memory (PIM) Accelerators: </span>
PIM architectures aim to reduce data movement by embedding compute capabilities within or near memory <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">20</a>, <a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">33</a>, <a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">46</a>, <a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">70</a>, <a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>]</cite>.
Many PIM designs leverage DRAM or emerging memory technologies to perform simple operations, typically integer or bitwise logic, in situ.
While effective for low-intensity workloads, PIM designs struggle when arithmetic intensity exceeds 1 Op/Byte, which is common during LLM inference.
PIM architectures are also poorly suited for floating-point operations or fine-grained programmability to support rotary embeddings, softmax, and normalization functions.</p>
</div>
<div id="S10.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S10.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Furthermore, the rise of block-quantized formats (e.g., BFP, MXFP) poses a major challenge for PIM.
These formats require dynamic exponent broadcasting, alignment, and decoding before arithmetic.
These steps involve conditional logic and variable indexing, which are difficult to implement in DRAM-compatible circuitry.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S10.F14" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18568v1/RELATED_WORK.svg" id="S10.F14.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/143;" width="476" height="143"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Fig. 14: </span>
A comparison of leading hardware platforms.
Speculative decoding throughput for Llama3-70B based on published data <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">57</a>, <a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">52</a>, <a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>, <a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">64</a>]</cite>.
</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S10.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S10.p6.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S10.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">Comparison Under Speculative Decoding: </span>

Speculative decoding is an increasingly common technique used in LLM inference to reduce token generation latency by leveraging a lightweight “draft” model to predict multiple tokens ahead.
These predicted tokens are then validated by a larger “target” model; if the predictions are correct, several tokens can be committed in parallel.
This approach may be challenging
because it increases the arithmetic intensity of each query.</p>
</div>
<div id="S10.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S10.p7.1" class="ltx_p">Industry accelerators often report performance under speculative decoding.
We evaluate the RPU using a comparable speculative decode setup.
In our evaluation, we adopt an 8-token lookahead configuration in which a Llama3-8B draft model proposes tokens for a Llama3-70B target model.
On average, 4.6 tokens are accepted per speculative window <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">38</a>]</cite>, accelerating end-to-end inference by 1.8×.
Figure <a href="#S10.F14" title="Fig. 14 ‣ X Related Work ‣ RPU – A Reasoning Processing Unit" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">14</span></a> compares our speculative performance to publicly reported numbers from NVIDIA H200 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">57</a>]</cite>, SambaNova SN40L <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">52</a>]</cite>, Groq <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>]</cite>, and Cerebras WSE-3 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">64</a>]</cite>.
The RPU-200U configuration is lower latency than all evaluated systems.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S11" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">XI </span><span id="S11.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Conclusion</span></h2>

<div id="S11.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S11.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Just as custom logic design led to configurable ASIC toolchains and foundry ecosystems, memory must follow a similar path.
Commodity DRAMs no longer aligns with the needs of modern inference systems.
Memory should be treated not as fixed infrastructure, but as a key dimension of system specialization.
With chiplet-based integration, customizable memory is not only desirable but also practical.
It allows system designers to co-optimize bandwidth, capacity, and energy by tailoring the design, packaging, and tuning of DRAM components for specific workloads.
The RPU system embraces this philosophy by co-designing its memory architecture with compute and interconnect, treating memory not as a constraint but as an opportunity for specialization.</p>
</div>
</section>

              d="M224 160C224 107 267 64 320 64C373 64 416 107 416 160L416 163.6C416 179.3 403.3 192 387.6 192L252.5 192C236.8 192 224.1 179.3 224.1 163.6L224.1 160zM569.6 172.8C580.2 186.9 577.3 207 563.2 217.6L465.4 290.9C470.7 299.8 474.7 309.6 477.2 320L576 320C593.7 320 608 334.3 608 352C608 369.7 593.7 384 576 384L480 384L480 416C480 418.6 479.9 421.3 479.8 423.9L563.2 486.4C577.3 497 580.2 517.1 569.6 531.2C559 545.3 538.9 548.2 524.8 537.6L461.7 490.3C438.5 534.5 395.2 566.5 344 574.2L344 344C344 330.7 333.3 320 320 320C306.7 320 296 330.7 296 344L296 574.2C244.8 566.5 201.5 534.5 178.3 490.3L115.2 537.6C101.1 548.2 81 545.3 70.4 531.2C59.8 517.1 62.7 497 76.8 486.4L160.2 423.9C160.1 421.3 160 418.7 160 416L160 384L64 384C46.3 384 32 369.7 32 352C32 334.3 46.3 320 64 320L162.8 320C165.3 309.6 169.3 299.8 174.6 290.9L76.8 217.6C62.7 207 59.8 186.9 70.4 172.8C81 158.7 101.1 155.8 115.2 166.4L224 248C236.3 242.9 249.8 240 264 240L376 240C390.2 240 403.7 242.8 416 248L524.8 166.4C538.9 155.8 559 158.7 569.6 172.8z" />
          </svg>)</span> button, located in the page header.</li>
    </ul>
    <p><strong>Tip:</strong> You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.</p>
    <p>Our team has already identified <a class="ltx_ref" href="https://github.com/arXiv/html_feedback/issues"
        target="_blank">the following issues</a>. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we
      may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability
      should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for
      all.</p>
    <p>Have a free development cycle? Help support accessibility at arXiv! Our collaborators at LaTeXML maintain a <a
        class="ltx_ref" href="https://github.com/brucemiller/LaTeXML/wiki/Porting-LaTeX-packages-for-LaTeXML"
        target="_blank">list of packages that need conversion</a>, and welcome <a class="ltx_ref"
        href="https://github.com/brucemiller/LaTeXML/issues" target="_blank">developer contributions</a>.</p>
